Concrete Patio Cost

How much does a concrete patio cost?

A concrete patio runs $6 to $10 per square foot installed in 2026, and most projects land between $7 and $9. A patio is the cheapest of the flatwork pours — thin, lightly reinforced, and easy to access.

Patio specs

How to spec a patio that performs

The standard patio specification

  • 4 inches of concrete — the standard residential minimum, and enough for foot traffic, furniture, and a grill
  • 3,000–3,500 PSI concrete; 4,000 PSI with 5–7% air entrainment in freeze-thaw climates
  • 4 inches of compacted crushed stone base
  • Welded wire mesh or fiber reinforcement, at mid-depth
  • Control joints every 8–10 feet, sawn within a few hours of finishing
  • Curing compound applied as soon as the surface water is gone

The IRC does not regulate exterior patios. ACI 330R-08 states there is no benefit in building slabs less than 4 inches thick.

Where to go thicker

  • Hot tubs and outdoor kitchens — thicken to 6 inches under the concentrated load area with #4 rebar at 12 in on center
  • Heavy planters — 6 inches with #4 rebar
  • Freeze-thaw climates — stay at 4 inches but upgrade to 4,000 PSI with air entrainment; air matters more than thickness

How much does a concrete slab cost per square foot?

A standard residential concrete slab runs $6 to $12 per square foot installed in 2026, with most projects landing near $8 per square foot. That figure includes ready-mix concrete, delivery, a compacted gravel base, forms, reinforcement, placing and finishing labor, control joints, and curing compound — but not major excavation, permits, or decorative finishes.

The cost per square foot breaks down roughly like this:

  • Concrete material: $2–$3.30 per sq ft
  • Labor (pour and finish): $3–$8 per sq ft — usually the single biggest line
  • Site prep and forms: $1–$2.50 per sq ft
  • Reinforcement: $0.20–$2.00 per sq ft
  • Curing and sealer: $0.25–$1.00 per sq ft

Small slabs cost more per square foot than large ones because the truck delivery, crew minimum, and forms are fixed costs spread over less area. A 10 x 10 pad typically runs $8.50–$15.00 per sq ft, while a 40 x 60 driveway lands closer to $6.50–$12.50 per sq ft. Decorative work — stamped, colored, or exposed aggregate — adds $3 to $10 per sq ft on top.

One important caveat about scope. Published per-square-foot figures disagree by nearly 40%, and the reason is that they measure different things. A quote at $6 per sq ft is often scoped to exclude delivery fees, control joints, curing compound, and site prep — real costs that a complete project pays. Price the same scope before comparing two bids; a lower number is not a better deal if it is missing items.

How much does it cost to pour a concrete slab?

Pouring a concrete slab costs $4 to $14 per square foot installed, depending on thickness, reinforcement, finish, and how much site work the ground needs. A plain broom-finished 4-inch slab on a flat, accessible site sits at the low end; a thick, reinforced slab on ground that needs grading and fill sits at the high end.

Realistic totals for common sizes at $6–$12 per sq ft:

  • 10 x 10 pad (100 sq ft): $600–$1,200
  • 12 x 12 pad (144 sq ft): $864–$1,730
  • 20 x 20 slab (400 sq ft): $2,400–$4,800
  • 24 x 24 garage pad (576 sq ft): $3,500–$9,000
  • 30 x 30 slab (900 sq ft): $3,600–$7,200

A useful shortcut: the concrete itself is only about 25% of an installed slab. Labor is usually 45–55%. That is why a slab quoted at $4 per square foot for materials alone is not out of line — it simply excludes the crew.

How many bags of concrete do I need?

Divide the pour's volume in cubic feet by the finished yield of one bag, then round up. Standard yields are 0.30 ft³ for a 40 lb bag, 0.45 ft³ for a 60 lb bag, and 0.60 ft³ for an 80 lb bag.

Bags = ceil( volume in ft³ x (1 + waste%) / yield per bag )

One cubic yard of concrete equals about 90 bags of 40 lb, 60 bags of 60 lb, or 45 bags of 80 lb mix.

Worked example — a 10 x 10 ft slab at 4 inches thick:

  • Volume = 10 x 10 x (4 ÷ 12) = 33.3 ft³ = 1.23 yd³
  • With 10% waste: 36.7 ft³
  • 80 lb bags: ceil(36.7 ÷ 0.60) = 62 bags
  • 60 lb bags: ceil(36.7 ÷ 0.45) = 82 bags

Bagged mix stops making sense above roughly 1 cubic yard. Past about 45 bags of 80 lb mix, hauling, mixing, and pouring by hand costs more in time and labor than a ready-mix truck — and cold joints between batches are far more likely.

How many yards of concrete do I need?

Multiply length by width by thickness in feet, then divide by 27. There are 27 cubic feet in a cubic yard.

Cubic yards = (Length ft x Width ft x Thickness in ÷ 12) ÷ 27
Shortcut: Cubic yards = (sq ft x thickness in) ÷ 324

For a 20 x 20 ft slab at 4 inches: (400 x 4) ÷ 324 = 4.94 cubic yards. Add 5–10% for waste and order about 5.5 yards.

As a rule of thumb, one cubic yard covers about 81 sq ft at 4 inches, 65 sq ft at 5 inches, 54 sq ft at 6 inches, and 41 sq ft at 8 inches. A standard ready-mix truck carries about 10 cubic yards.

How thick should a concrete slab be?

Spec it by load, not by rule of thumb:

  • 3.5–4 in — walkways, garden paths, patios, shed and AC pads (foot traffic only)
  • 4 in — the standard residential minimum; patios and light floors
  • 5 in — residential driveways and garage floors carrying passenger cars or half-ton pickups
  • 6 in — driveways taking trucks and RVs, heavy equipment pads, and commercial slabs
  • 8 in — post-tensioned, heavily loaded, or industrial slabs

For code: the International Residential Code (R506.1) sets a 3.5-inch minimum for slab-on-grade floors in habitable space, and most jurisdictions amend that to 4 inches. The IRC does not regulate exterior patios and walkways, though local codes often do govern driveways — published driveway standards run from 4 to 7 inches depending on the municipality.

ACI 330R-08 puts it plainly: "As a practical matter, there is no benefit in building slabs less than 4 in. (100 mm) thick." Thickness is the cheapest structural upgrade available — bending capacity scales with the square of thickness, so 4 in to 6 in is 50% more concrete but roughly 2.25x the bending resistance.

What PSI concrete do I need for a slab?

Match the strength to the exposure and the load:

  • 3,000 PSI — interior slabs, basement floors, and shop floors that never see salt or freezing
  • 3,500 PSI — standard patios, sidewalks, and exterior residential work
  • 4,000 PSI — driveways, garage floors, and any exterior slab in a freeze-thaw climate, specified with 5–7% air entrainment
  • 4,500–5,000 PSI — heavy vehicle pads, warehouse slabs, and structural work per ACI 318

ACI 332 requires 4,000 PSI with air entrainment for exterior residential slabs in freeze-thaw zones. Each 500 PSI step up adds roughly $4–$10 per cubic yard, which is cheap insurance against scaling and spalling. In freeze-thaw climates, air entrainment matters more than an extra inch of thickness — 3,000 PSI slabs without air can scale badly within 5 to 10 years.

How much does a concrete patio cost?

A concrete patio costs $6 to $10 per square foot installed in 2026, and most projects land between $7 and $9.

Typical totals:

  • 10 x 10 patio (100 sq ft): $600–$1,000
  • 12 x 12 patio (144 sq ft): $864–$1,440
  • 16 x 20 patio (320 sq ft): $1,900–$3,200
  • 20 x 20 patio (400 sq ft): $2,400–$4,400

A patio is the cheapest of the flatwork pours because it is thin (4 inches), light on reinforcement, and easy to access. Decorative finishes change the number: stamped patios run $10–$22 per sq ft, and exposed aggregate runs $8–$15.

The spread above reflects scope, not just size. A quote that excludes delivery, control joints, curing compound, and site prep lands near the bottom; a complete project lands near the top.

How much does a 20x20 concrete patio cost?

A 20 x 20 ft patio covers 400 square feet. Installed, expect $2,400 to $4,400 for a standard 4-inch broom-finish slab, with most fully-scoped projects landing near $3,200–$4,400.

Where the money goes on a 400 sq ft patio:

  • Ready-mix concrete (4.94 yd³ + 10% waste): $845–$930
  • Delivery plus short-load fee: $180–$320
  • 4 in compacted gravel base: $300–$760
  • Forms: $180–$360
  • Welded wire mesh: $80–$360
  • Placing and finishing labor: $1,200–$3,200
  • Control joints and curing compound: $180–$460

That is about $8 per square foot all-in. If your quote comes in materially higher, check whether the estimate assumed 4 inches or 6 inches, and whether a decorative finish or a pump is included.

How thick should a concrete patio be?

Four inches is the standard, and it handles everything a residential patio throws at it — people, furniture, a grill, and a hot tub on a thickened section.

The IRC does not actually regulate exterior patios, though the ACI 330R-08 guidance is worth quoting: "As a practical matter, there is no benefit in building slabs less than 4 in. (100 mm) thick."

For a patio, use 3,000–3,500 PSI concrete on 4 inches of compacted gravel, with welded wire mesh or fiber reinforcement. That combination is the industry standard for a patio slab.

Two exceptions where you should go thicker:

  • Hot tubs or outdoor kitchens — thicken to 6 inches under the concentrated load area with #4 rebar at 12 in on center.
  • Freeze-thaw climates — stay at 4 inches but specify 4,000 PSI with 5–7% air entrainment. Air entrainment matters more than thickness here.

Thickening a patio is cheap. Retrofitting a 4-inch slab to 6 inches after it has cracked is not.

How much does a concrete patio cost per square foot?

A concrete patio runs $7 to $12 per square foot installed in 2026.

  • 12 x 12 ft (144 sq ft) — $1,000 to $1,700
  • 16 x 16 ft (256 sq ft) — $1,800 to $3,100
  • 16 x 20 ft (320 sq ft) — $2,200 to $3,800
  • 20 x 20 ft (400 sq ft) — $2,800 to $4,800

A standard patio is 4 inches thick on a 4-inch compacted base with welded wire mesh, and it carries no vehicle load — which is why it sits below a driveway on the same square foot.

A stamped or colored surface adds $5 to $12 per square foot. The concrete costs the same; the extra is labor for the pattern and the sealer.

Do I need rebar in a concrete patio?

Usually welded wire mesh rather than rebar — and sometimes neither.

For a 4 inch patio on well-compacted, stable ground with furniture and foot traffic, most builders use 6 x 6 inch welded wire mesh. It costs a fraction of rebar, it does not rust the way rebar can at the surface, and it holds the slab together against shrinkage cracking.

Use #3 rebar at 24 inches on center instead where the patio spans, sits over fill, or abuts the house and needs to stay level with the door threshold.

Two things matter more than the material choice. The mesh or rebar must sit in the bottom third of the slab, and it must have at least 2 inches of cover from the edge. Mesh laid directly on the base will rust through in a few wet winters.

Mesh is supplied in 5 x 7 ft sheets, so a 20 x 20 ft patio needs about 12 sheets with the laps lapped one full mesh spacing.

How much does an irregular-shaped concrete patio cost?

Shape affects cost mostly through formwork, not through the concrete itself. Concrete is priced by volume, so a curved patio uses the same concrete per square foot as a square one. The difference is the labor to set and hold curved forms and to finish the edges.

A straight-edged 16 x 20 ft patio at 4 inches is 320 sq ft and about 2.4 cubic yards. A curved patio of the same area needs roughly 10 to 20% more labor because the forms are built from flexible or cut sections rather than straight boards, and the edges are harder to screed.

Expect a curved or freeform patio to land at $9 to $15 per square foot rather than $7 to $12.

Calculate the volume by breaking the shape into rectangles and triangles and adding the areas — for example, a rectangle 20 x 12 ft plus a triangle with a 20 ft base and 6 ft height gives 240 + 60 = 300 sq ft. The calculator's Triangle and Custom modes do this directly.

Where do control joints go in a concrete patio?

Space them so no panel is wider than 10 feet in any direction for a 4 inch slab. Most patios work out to one joint down the middle and one across, dividing the slab into four roughly square panels.

A 20 x 20 ft patio wants joints at the 10 foot marks in both directions — four panels. A 12 x 16 ft patio wants one joint across the long side at 8 feet and one down the middle of the remaining panel.

For a patio with an L-shape or a curve, run the joints so they continue from the edge of the slab, and keep the panels as close to square as you can. Long, narrow panels crack more readily than square ones.

Cut the joints within 1 to 4 hours of finishing, to a depth of 1 inch — one quarter of a 4 inch slab. Seal every joint with a flexible polyurethane or polysulfide sealer, and keep it maintained. A failed joint is where water gets in, and water gets in is how a patio ends up with a chunk missing two winters later.

How long does a concrete patio take to cure?

24 to 48 hours before walking, 7 days before setting furniture on it, and 28 days before sealing or heavy loading.

Concrete gains roughly 50% of its final strength in the first 3 days and reaches design strength at 28 days. The practical difference between a patio and a driveway is that a patio carries furniture and foot traffic, not vehicles — so 7 days is usually enough for normal use.

Keep the curing compound on for the full period, and do not let the surface dry out. Concrete cures by hydrating, not by drying. If it loses moisture too fast in the first days, the surface will crust and dust.

Two avoidable mistakes: moving furniture back within the first 48 hours, which leaves marks, and applying a sealer before 28 days, which can trap moisture and cause surface scaling.

How much more does a stamped concrete patio cost?

Stamping adds $5 to $12 per square foot over standard broom finish. A 320 sq ft patio moves from roughly $2,200 to $3,800–$6,600 depending on the pattern.

The cost is almost entirely labor. The concrete itself is the same 3,500 PSI mix, and the coloring is either an integral pigment broadcast into the surface or a chemical stain applied after the pour. The real cost is the crew working the mat into the soft concrete — every square foot has to be stamped before it hardens enough to reject the impression.

Two things drive the price up. Complex patterns with multiple textures and grout lines take far longer than a simple ashlar slate. Colored, sealed concrete adds a layer of work and a second material.

For comparison, stamped concrete runs well below pavers on installed cost, has no joints between units, and cannot shift or settle individually. Against pavers, the trade is a less forgiving repair story if the slab ever moves.

Can I pour a concrete patio myself?

Yes — a 10 x 10 patio at 4 inches is 1.23 cubic yards, which is one of the most realistic DIY pours there is. The labor is the hard part, not the arithmetic.

The realistic DIY sequence: excavate and compact a 4-inch base, lay the vapor barrier, set forms and mesh, order the concrete, pour and screed, float and finish, cut the joints, and cure. That is a full weekend for two people, and the screeding step is where inexperienced hands go wrong.

Three things to decide before starting. Do you have a way to move 4,050 lb of concrete? With ready-mix, that is a truck backing up to the forms. With bags, it is 62 trips in a wheelbarrow. Can you finish it in the working time? A 1.23 cubic yard pour is manageable; a 4 cubic yard pour is not a one-day beginner project.

And do you know where the control joints go before you start, not after. Once the concrete is down, the joints are where you put them.

Do I need a vapor barrier under a concrete patio?

Yes — 6 mil poly or a 10 mil vapor retarder goes under the slab, on top of the compacted base and under the reinforcement.

Its job is to stop moisture from the soil wicking up through the slab. That matters for three reasons: it stops damp rising into the finished surface and causing efflorescence, it keeps moisture away from the mesh or rebar so it does not corrode, and it stops the ground from pulling water out of the concrete during the cure.

A vapor retarder is not the same as waterproofing. It is a slowly-permeable sheet, designed to let the ground dry downward while stopping upward moisture movement. That is the correct choice for a slab-on-grade. A true waterproof membrane for a crawlspace or basement is a different product with a different installation.

Lay it flat with no wrinkles or tears, lap the seams generously, and seal the edges with tape or sealant. A 2-inch lap and a bead of sealant along the perimeter is standard practice.

Do not skip it. It is one of the cheapest items in the job and one of the hardest to retrofit.

How much does a 20 x 20 concrete patio cost?

A 20 x 20 ft patio at 4 inches with a 4-inch base and welded wire mesh costs $2,800 to $4,800 installed in 2026 — about $10.45 per square foot at the typical rate.

Material breakdown: 400 sq ft at 4 inches is 4.94 cubic yards, which is 245 bags of 80 lb mix or one ready-mix load of 5.43 yards with waste. Ready-mix runs about $842 plus $120 delivery.

Everything else on the bill: site prep $340, gravel base $500, forms $180, mesh $180, vapor barrier $80, labor $1,800, control joints $175 and curing compound $200.

A 20 x 20 patio needs four control joints — one across the middle in each direction — so no panel is wider than 10 feet.
